McPherson Eye Research Institute Madison United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract In congenital stationary night blindness, type 2 (CSNB2)—a disorder involving the Cav1.4 (L-type) Ca2+ channel—visual impairment is mild considering that Cav1.4 mediates synaptic release from rod and cone photoreceptors. Here, we addressed this conundrum using a Cav1.4 knockout (KO) mouse and a knock-in (G369i KI) mouse expressing a non-conducting Cav1.4. Surprisingly, Cav3 (T-type) Ca2+ currents were detected in cones of G369i KI mice and Cav1.4 KO mice but not in cones of wild-type mouse, ground squirrels, and macaque retina. Whereas Cav1.4 KO mice are blind, G369i KI mice exhibit normal photopic (i.e. cone-mediated) visual behavior. Cone synapses, which fail to form in Cav1.4 KO mice, are present, albeit enlarged, and with some errors in postsynaptic wiring in G369i KI mice. While Cav1.4 KO mice lack evidence of cone synaptic responses, electrophysiological recordings in G369i KI mice revealed nominal transmission from cones to horizontal cells and bipolar cells. In CSNB2, we propose that Cav3 channels maintain cone synaptic output provided that the nonconducting role of Cav1.4 in cone synaptogenesis remains intact. Our findings reveal an unexpected form of homeostatic plasticity that relies on a non-canonical role of an ion channel. ## Introduction At the first synapse in the visual pathway, graded electrical signals produced in rod and cone photoreceptors gate the release of glutamate onto postsynaptic neurons. Photoreceptor synapses are specialized with a vesicle-associated ribbon organelle and postsynaptic neurites of horizontal and bipolar cells that invaginate deep within the terminal (Haverkamp et al., 2000). A variety of proteins interact with the ribbon and synaptic vesicles near release sites (i.e. active zones) (Mercer and Thoreson, 2011). The importance of these proteins for vision is illustrated by the numerous inherited retinal diseases linked to mutations in their encoding genes (Frederick and Zenisek, 2023). One such gene is CACNA1F, which encodes the voltage-gated Ca2+ (Cav) channel expressed in retinal photoreceptors, Cav1.4 (Mansergh et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2006). Among the sub-family of Cav1 L-type channels, Cav1.4 exhibits unusually slow inactivation that is well-matched for supporting the tonic, Ca2+-dependent release of glutamate from photoreceptor synaptic terminals in darkness (Singh et al., 2006; Wahl-Schott et al., 2006). More than 200 mutations in CACNA1F cause vision disorders including congenital stationary night blindness type 2 (CSNB2) (Bech-Hansen et al., 1998; Strom et al., 1998). These mutations are broadly categorized as producing a gain of function or loss of function in Cav1.4 (Waldner et al., 2018). How these mutations in CACNA1F lead to the variable clinical phenotypes of CSNB2 is largely unknown. Symptoms may include strabismus, low visual acuity, and in many cases, night blindness (Boycott et al., 2000; Zeitz et al., 2015). The latter suggests a primary defect in rod pathways, which is surprising given that Cav1.4 KO mice are completely blind and lack any evidence of either rod or cone synaptic responses (Mansergh et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013; Regus-Leidig et al., 2014). A major caveat is that rod and cone synapses do not form in Cav1.4 KO mice (Liu et al., 2013; Regus-Leidig et al., 2014; Zabouri and Haverkamp, 2013; Raven et al., 2008). Thus, Cav1.4 KO mice are not suitable for studies of how CACNA1F mutations differentially affect rod and cone pathways or for efforts to uncover how the biophysical properties of Cav1.4 shape photoreceptor synaptic release properties. Here, we overcome this hurdle with a knock-in mouse strain (G369i KI) expressing a non-conducting mutant form of Cav1.4 (Maddox et al., 2020). We show that, although greatly impaired, cone synapses and downstream signaling through cone pathways can support photopic visual function in G369i KI mice. This novel mechanism requires the ability of the Cav1.4 protein, independent of its Ca2+ conductance, to nucleate the assembly of cone ribbon synapses and involves an aberrant Cav3 (T-type) conductance that appears when Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are compromised. ## Results ### Cone pedicles and ribbons are present in G369i KI mice but not in Cav1.4 KO mice The G369i mutation results in an insertion of a glycine residue in a transmembrane domain, which prevents Ca2+ permeation through Cav1.4 (Maddox et al., 2020). The presence of rod synapses in G369i KI mice but not Cav1.4 KO mice indicates that the Cav1.4 protein and not its Ca2+ conductance is required for rod synapse assembly (Maddox et al., 2020). To test if this is also true for cones, we performed immunofluorescence and confocal analyses using antibodies against cone arrestin (CAR) and CtBP2 to label cone terminals (i.e. pedicles) and ribbons, respectively (Figure 1). In Cav1.4 KO mouse retinas, cone pedicles were shrunken and retracted into the outer nuclear layer (ONL, Figure 1a) with little evidence of elongated ribbons (Figure 1b). In contrast, cone pedicles in G369i KI mice were normally localized in the outer plexiform layer (OPL, Figure 1a) and were populated by multiple ribbons that were associated with labeling for Cav1.4 (Figure 1b). Some abnormalities were apparent in G369i KI cone pedicles, such as extremely elongated ribbons and telodendria extending toward the inner nuclear layer (Figure 1b). These results indicate that Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for the integrity of ribbons and the pedicle but are necessary for their overall refinement. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94908/elife-94908-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** Confocal images of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) and outer plexiform layer (OPL) of retina from wild-type (WT), G369i KI, and Cav1.4 KO mice that were labeled with antibodies against cone arrestin (CAR), CtBP2, and Cav1.4. Rod-associated CtBP2 and Cav1.4 labeling was removed for clarity. ### Cav3 channel activity is present in cones of G369i KI and Cav1.4 KO mice but not WT mice, ground squirrels, or macaque retina A prevailing yet unsupported hypothesis regarding the relatively mild visual phenotypes in CSNB2 is that additional Cav subtypes may compensate for Cav1.4 loss-of-function in cones. If so, then Ca2+ currents (ICa) mediated by these subtypes should be evident in cones of Cav1.4 KO and G369i KI mice. To test this, we performed patch clamp recordings of cones in retinal slices of adult WT, G369i KI, and Cav1.4 KO mice under conditions designed to isolate ICa. During voltage ramps in WT cones, ICa activated around –50 mV and peaked near –20 mV, consistent with the properties of Cav1.4 (Figure 2a–d). While not observed in rods of G369i KI or Cav1.4 KO mice (Maddox et al., 2020), a small-amplitude ICa that activated around –60 mV and peaked near –35 mV was detected in cones of these mice (Figure 2a–d). To uncover this low voltage-activated ICa, we used a faster voltage ramp (0.5 mV/ms) than in the previous study of G369i KI rods (~0.15 mV/ms) Maddox et al., 2020. With this faster voltage ramp, ICa was not apparent in G369i KI rods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Therefore, the aberrant ICa is an adaptation to Cav1.4 loss-of-function in cones but not rods. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94908/elife-94908-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** (a) Representative traces of ICa evoked by voltage ramps. We next used step depolarizations to identify the type of Cav channel underlying ICa in G369i KI and Cav1.4 KO cones. Analysis of current-voltage (I-V) and conductance-voltage (G-V) relationships revealed a significant, hyperpolarizing shift (~10 mV) in the voltage of half-maximal activation (Vh) in G369i KI cones (Figure 2c and d; Table 1). ICa in G369i KI cones was not sustained as in WT cones but inactivated rapidly during 500 ms step depolarizations (Figure 2e). For G369i KI cones, the overlay of the conductance-voltage (Figure 2d) and inactivation curves revealed a sizeable window current (Figure 2f). However, in recordings of WT mouse cone somas, we did not observe a low-voltage activated component in the I-V or G-V curves that would be indicative of a Cav3 subtype (Figure 2c and d). To further test for a Cav3 contribution to ICa in WT mouse cones, we used a double pulse voltage protocol where ICa was evoked before (P1) and after (P2) a 500 ms step to –60 mV (Figure 2g). With this protocol, the inactivation of Cav3 channels by the –60 mV step should lead to a reduction in the amplitude of the P2 vs the P1 current. While such a reduction was clearly evident in cones of G369i KI mice (i.e. P2/P1 <1), there was no significant difference in the P2 and P1 currents in cones of WT mice (Figure 2g–i). We also used antagonists selective for Cav1 and Cav3 channels (isradipine and ML 218, respectively). As expected, ICa in WT cones was significantly but incompletely suppressed by isradipine (Figure 3a and b). The Vh of the I-V was similar before (–36.5±0.8 mV) and after (–38.3±1.8 mV) perfusion of isradipine (t(3,4)=0.90, p=0.43 by paired t-test), suggesting that the residual ICa after exposure to isradipine arose from unblocked Cav1.4 rather than Cav3 channels. While ML 218 modestly inhibited ICa in some WT cones, the effect was not statistically significant (Figure 3c and d) and could be attributed to weak activity on Cav1.4. In transfected HEK293T cells, ML 218 modestly inhibited ICa and caused a negative shift in the Vh for Cav1.4, in contrast to its strong inhibition of Cav3.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Finally, we recorded from ground squirrel and macaque cones, where the large amplitude of ICa facilitates pharmacological and biophysical analyses. Consistent with its actions on Cav1.4 in WT mouse cones (Figure 3b) and transfected HEK293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), ML 218 caused an insignificant inhibition of peak ICa (–7.0 ± 20.8%, n=6 cones) as well as a negative shift in the voltage-dependence of activation in ground squirrel cones (ΔV1/2 = -1.16 ± 0.94 mV, n=6, mean ± SD, p=0.029, t-test; Figure 4a and b). By contrast, the application of isradipine dramatically suppressed ICa in cones in various regions of the ground squirrel retina (Figure 4c and d). Subsequent application of ML 218 did not reveal a Cav3-like current: the I-V and G-V of the isradipine + ML 218-sensitive current were shifted in the positive rather than the negative direction relative to the isradipine-sensitive current (Figure 4c–g). This result is consistent with the time- and voltage-dependent block of Cav1 channels by dihydropyridine antagonists such as isradipine (Koschak et al., 2003). As a positive control, we confirmed that ML 218 blocked a prominent Cav3-type current in ground squirrel type 3 a OFF cone bipolar cells (Figure 4h and i). In recordings of macaque cone pedicles, we compared the properties of ICa using a holding voltage of –90 mV or –50 mV, the latter of which should inactivate Cav3 channels (Figure 5a). There was no difference in the I-V or G-V relationships obtained at these holding voltages (Figure 5b–e). As in WT mouse cones (Figure 2g–i), there was also no difference in ICa recorded before and after an inactivating pulse to –60 mV (Figure 5f and g). To test whether the appearance of the Cav3-mediated ICa in G369i KI cones could result from an increase in the expression of a specific Cav3 subtype (i.e. Cav3.1, Cav3.2, or Cav3.3), we initially tried labeling with commercially available antibodies against Cav3.2. However, the data were unreliable since these antibodies produced a similar labeling pattern in Cav3.2 KO retinal tissue (data not shown). As an alternative, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on cells isolated from the retina of WT and G369i KI mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). We sequenced 28,782 cells and, with unsupervised clustering at resolution = 0.5, we grouped the cells into 20 clusters. Clusters 8 and 16 were identified as cones based on the expression of cone marker genes (e.g. Opn1sw, Opn1mw, Arr3, Gnat2). Consistent with previous studies (Davison et al., 2022; Williams et al., 2022), Cacna1h encoding the Cav3.2 subtype was the major Cav3 transcript expressed in WT mouse cones. There was no significant difference in Cacna1h expression between WT and G369i KI cones according to this analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Thus, the enhanced activity of Cav3 channels in cones of G369i KI mice results from a mechanism other than increased transcription of Cacna1h. ### Cone synapses are enlarged with some errors in postsynaptic wiring in G369i KI mice The replacement of Cav1.4 with Cav3 as the primary conduit for Ca2+ influx in G369i KI cones allowed us to dissect the importance of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals for the molecular and structural organization of the cone synapse. To this end, we first analyzed WT and G369i KI cone synapses by immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy. Presynaptic proteins such as bassoon and members of the postsynaptic signaling complex in depolarizing (ON) cone bipolar cells (GPR179, mGluR6, and TRPM1 Martemyanov and Sampath, 2017) were enriched near cone ribbons in G369i KI mice as in WT mice (Figure 6a). Compared to WT mice, the labeled structures in G369i KI mice occupied a larger volume (Figure 6b and c) but were of lower intensity (Figure 6d), suggesting an increase in the spread rather than in the levels of synaptic proteins. Unlike in WT mice, the volume of presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins increased linearly with the volume of the pedicle in G369i KI mice (Figure 6e–i). These results show that the molecular determinants of the cone synapse can assemble in G369i KI mice but change in their sub-synaptic distribution in ways that correlate with the expansion of the cone pedicle. ![Figure 6.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/94908/elife-94908-fig6-v1.jpg) **Figure 6.:** (a) Confocal images of the outer plexiform layer (OPL) of WT and G369i KI mice labeled with antibodies against cone arrestin (CAR) and proteins that are presynaptic (CtBP2, bassoon) or postsynaptic (GPR179, TRPM1, mGluR6). The cone synapse is structurally complex, with the dendritic tips of two horizontal cells and an intervening ON cone bipolar cell invaginating deeply into the pedicle near the ribbon (Haverkamp et al., 2000). In the retina, ablation or degeneration of photoreceptors triggers various postsynaptic mechanisms that maintain some level of visual function in rod or cone pathways. These include remodeling of bipolar cell dendrites and their synapses (Beier et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2020; Leinonen et al., 2020) as well as changes in the sensitivity of bipolar cells to photoreceptor input and inhibitory modulation (Leinonen et al., 2020; Care et al., 2020). To our knowledge, this study provides the first evidence for a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity that originates within photoreceptors. Using Cav1.4 KO and G369i KI mice, we identify the upregulation of a Cav3 conductance as a common response to Cav1.4 loss-of-function in cones. However, Cav3 channels can only compensate for Cav1.4 loss-of-function if the basic aspects of cone synapse structure are maintained through an expression of the G369i mutant channel. Thus, our results also highlight a crucial, non-conducting role for the Cav1.4 protein that allows cone synapses to function in the absence of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals. ### A non-canonical role for Cav1.4 in regulating cone synapse assembly As shown for rod synapses (Maddox et al., 2020), ribbons and other components of the pre- and post-synaptic complex assemble at cone synapses in G369i KI mice (Figures 1, 6 and 7). Cav3 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for this process since their presence in Cav1.4 KO cones is not accompanied by any semblance of ribbon synapses (Figure 1b). An intimate relationship between Cav1.4 and ribbons is supported by the colocalization of Cav1.4 and puncta resembling ribbon precursor spheres in the developing OPL (Liu et al., 2013). Cav1.4 interacts directly or indirectly with a variety of ribbon synapse-associated proteins including RIM (Kiyonaka et al., 2007), CAST/ERC2 (Kiyonaka et al., 2012), bassoon (tom Dieck et al., 2005), unc119 Alpadi et al., 2008; Haeseleer, 2008; Haeseleer et al., 2004, and a major component of the ribbon, RIBEYE (Schmitz et al., 2000). Cav1.4 could pioneer sites of ribbon assembly perhaps by serving as a docking or nucleation site for the active zone. At the same time, ribbon-associated proteins help cluster Cav1.4 near ribbons since knockout of these proteins in mice leads to fewer presynaptic Cav1.4 channels and in some cases shortened ribbons (tom Dieck et al., 2012). Regardless of the mechanism, our findings show that the formation of photoreceptor synaptic complexes does not require Ca2+ influx through Cav1.4 channels. ### Functional Cav3 channels are present in cones in the absence of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals Our drop-seq analysis aligns with previous studies indicating that Cacna1h is expressed at extremely low levels compared to Cacna1f in WT mouse cones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Williams et al., 2022; Macosko et al., 2015). However, in contrast to recordings of WT mouse cone pedicles in a previous study (Davison et al., 2022), we found no evidence for Cav3-mediated currents in somatic recordings of cones in WT mice (Figures 2 and 3). We do not feel the discrepancy results from the different recording configurations given the electrically compact nature of cones. Moreover, recordings from macaque cone pedicles and from the ellipsoids of cylindrically shaped ground squirrel cones also did not reveal a Cav3-mediated current (Figures 4 and 5). We acknowledge that there are caveats of the pharmacological approach used in our study as well as the previous work (Davison et al., 2022). For example, dihydropyridine antagonists such as isradipine have relatively low affinity for some Cav1 subtypes, including Cav1.4 Koschak et al., 2003; Koschak et al., 2001, and have strongly voltage-dependent blocking properties. At a holding voltage of –90 mV, isradipine at 1 μM causes only ~80% inhibition of Cav1.4 with a greater block at depolarized voltages (Koschak et al., 2003), which agrees with our recordings of cones in WT mice (Figure 3a) and ground squirrels (Figure 4b–e). Moreover, in the low micromolar range, Cav3 blockers such as Z944 Tringham et al., 2012 and ML 218 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) have nonspecific effects on Cav1 current amplitude and activation voltage. Thus, Cav channels mediating an ICa that is suppressed by Cav3 blockers and spared by dihydropyridines at negative voltages may be mistakenly categorized as Cav3 subtypes. In our experiments, the biophysical properties of the isradipine-sensitive ICa in cones of WT mice and ground squirrels resembled only those of Cav1, whereas those of the ML 218-sensitive ICa in cones of G369i KI mice resembled only those of Cav3. Therefore, we favor the interpretation that Cav3 contributes to ICa in mouse cones only upon silencing of Cav1.4 either by KO of the corresponding protein or by silencing its conductance. Since Cacna1h expression was similar in WT and G369i KI cones (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), what causes the increased Cav3 channel activity in the latter? Among the Cav3 subtypes, Cav3.2 is uniquely sensitive to post-translational modifications that facilitate the opening of the channel and/or its cell surface trafficking (Cai et al., 2021). For example, Cav3.2 interacts with the deubiquitinating enzyme USP5 which enhances levels of Cav3.2 protein levels by suppressing its proteasomal degradation (García-Caballero et al., 2014). In addition, Cav3.2 is phosphorylated by calmodulin-dependent kinase II Welsby et al., 2003 and cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Gomez et al., 2020), which enhances channel activation and current density, respectively. Further interrogation of our drop-seq dataset could illuminate novel Cav3.2-regulatory pathways that are modified in G369i KI cones. ### Consequences of Cav1.4 loss of function and relevance for CSNB2 Despite having the same complement of proteins as in WT mice, cone synapses in G369i KI mice were enlarged and made errors in postsynaptic partner selection (Figures 6 and 7). While I-V curves indicate similar peak ICa amplitudes in cones of WT and G369i KI mice near the membrane potential of cones in darkness (−45 to –50 mV Ingram et al., 2019, Figure 2a and c), the strong inactivation of Cav3 channels and/or reduced Ca2+ release from intracellular stores likely account for the greatly diminished Ca2+ signals in G369i KI pedicles (Figure 9). Paradoxically, reductions in presynaptic Ca2+ in rod photoreceptors correlated with illumination-dependent shrinkage of ribbons in vivo and in vitro (Dembla et al., 2020; Spiwoks-Becker et al., 2004; Regus-Leidig et al., 2010). However, ribbon synapse size increases with low presynaptic Ca2+ in zebrafish sensory hair cells Sheets et al., 2012. The mechanism involves decreased mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake and an increase in the redox state of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+/NADH ratio) (Wong et al., 2019). Cav3 Ca2+ signals may decay too quickly in G369i KI cones (Figure 9) to enable mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake or other mechanisms that trim ribbons. An intriguing result was the linear increase in ribbon synapse size with pedicle volume in G369i KI but not in WT mice (Figure 6e–i), which could represent a form of homeostatic synaptic scaling as has been demonstrated at the neuromuscular junction (Goel et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2020). Similarly, the presence of some non-invaginating contacts with incorrect partner pairings in G369i KI mice (Figure 7, Table 2) could be an attempt to increase synaptic connectivity to compensate for weakened synaptic output. Consistent with this possibility, diminished presynaptic Ca2+ signals and non-invaginating cone synapses also characterize the retina of mice lacking the extracellular α2δ−4 subunit of Cav1.4 (Kerov et al., 2018). The cone synapses of G369i KI mice and α2δ−4 KO mice are clearly functional given that photopic visual behavior is preserved in both mouse strains Figure 10e and f; Kerov et al., 2018 and, in the case of G369i KI mice, HCs exhibit EPSCs whose amplitude decreases with light and AMPA/kainate receptor blockade (Figure 8). Defects in cone synaptic transmission that correlate with aberrant cone synapse morphology and connectivity also typify a mouse strain with a gain-of-function mutation in Cav1.4 linked to CSNB2 (Zanetti et al., 2021; Knoflach et al., 2013). Thus, balanced presynaptic Ca2+ signals may be needed to encode the correct post-synaptic wiring and structure of the cone synapse. In addition to structural abnormalities in cone synapses, the inability of Cav3 channels to support sustained presynaptic Ca2+ entry likely contributed to the impaired light responses in HCs and CBCs in G369i KI mice (Figures 8 and 10). Due to their slow activation and strong inactivation (Perez-Reyes et al., 2009), Cav3 channels are not expected to fuel the Ca2+ nanodomains that support fast and sustained components of release, both of which occur only at ribbon sites in cones (Snellman et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2008). Cav3 channels may also be located further from the ribbon than Cav1.4, thus lowering the efficiency of coupling to exocytosis. Regardless of the features that differentiate the contributions of Cav3 and Cav1.4 to cone synaptic release, our findings provide further support for the widely held view that Cav1 channels are well-suited to support transmission at ribbon-type synapses. Based on extremely heterogeneous clinical presentations, CSNB2 manifests as a spectrum of visual disorders that originate from various mutations in CACNA1F (Boycott et al., 2000; Bijveld et al., 2013). Even though some CSNB2 mutant Cav1.4 channels may traffic normally to the plasma membrane, many of these mutations are expected to produce non-functional, non-conducting Cav1.4 channels (Peloquin et al., 2007; Hoda et al., 2005). Yet, the visual phenotypes of CSNB2 patients are not as severe as the complete blindness in Cav1.4 KO mice, which lack any Cav1.4 protein expression and exhibit no signs of visual behavior (Figure 10e and f; Kerov et al., 2018). Collectively, our results suggest that G369i KI mice accurately model Cav1.4 channelopathies in CSNB2 patients that are characterized by a greater impairment in rod than in cone pathways. This interpretation is supported by our findings that G369i KI mice exhibit horizontal cell responses to bright but not dim illumination (Figure 8), ERG responses under conditions of light adaptation (Figure 10a–d) but not dark-adaptation (Maddox et al., 2020), and visual behavior under photopic but not scotopic conditions (Figure 10e and f). Together with the enlargement of synaptic sites, modest levels of synaptic release from cones of G369i KI mice may support the nominal transmission of visual information through cone pathways. G369i KI mice could also exhibit homeostatic alterations in the inner retina, which are known to support visual function when photoreceptor input is severely compromised (Shen et al., 2020; Leinonen et al., 2020; Care et al., 2020). Future studies of the retinal circuitry and visual behavior of G369i KI mice could identify compensatory pathways that are recruited upon Cav1.4 loss-of-function and how they might be targeted in novel therapies for CSNB2 and related disorders. Based on analyses of retinae from genetically modified mice, and from wild-type ground squirrel and macaque, employing microscopic imaging, electrophysiology, and pharmacological manipulations, this valuable study on the role of Cav1.4 calcium channels in cone photoreceptor cells (i) shows that the expression of a Cav1.4 variant lacking calcium conductivity supports the development of cone synapses beyond what is observed in the complete absence of Cav1.4, and (ii) indicates that the cone pathway can partially operate even without calcium flux through Cav1.4 channels, thus preserving behavioral responses under bright light. The evidence for the function of Cav1.4 protein in synapse development is convincing and in agreement with a closely related earlier study by the same authors on rod photoreceptors. The mechanism of compensation of Cav1.4 loss by Cav3 remains unclear but appears to involve post-transcriptional processes. As congenital Cav1.4 dysfunction can cause stationary night blindness, this work relates to a wide range of neuroscience topics, from synapse biology to neuro-ophthalmology.

Cav1.4 calcium channels control voltage-dependent calcium influx at photoreceptor synapses, and congenital loss of Cav1.4 function causes stationary night blindness CSNB2. Based on a broad portfolio of methodological approaches - genetic mouse models, immunolabeling and microscopic imaging, serial block-face-SEM, ERGs, and electrophysiology - the authors show that cone photoreceptor synapse development is strongly perturbed in the absence of Cav1.4 protein, and that expression of a nonconducting Cav1.4 channel mitigates these perturbations. Further data indicate that Cav3 channels are present, which, according to the authors, may compensate for the loss of Cav1.4 calcium currents and thus maintain cone synaptic transmission. These data, which are in agreement with a similar study by the same authors on rod photoreceptor synapses, help to explain what functional defects exactly cause CSNB2 and why it is accompanied by only mild visual impairment.

The strengths of the present study are its conceptual and experimental soundness, the broad spectrum of cutting-edge methodological approaches pursued, and the convincing differential analysis of mutant phenotypes. Weaknesses mainly concern the fact that the mechanism by which Cav3 channels might partially compensate for the loss of Cav1.4 calcium currents remains unclear.

results.result: Cav3 (T-type) Ca2+ currents are present in cones of G369i KI and Cav1.4 KO mice but absent in wild-type mice, ground squirrels, and macaque retina. The aberrant Cav3 current in mutant mouse cones exhibits biophysical properties characteristic of T-type channels (hyperpolarized activation, rapid inactivation, window current) and is sensitive to ML 218 but not isradipine, while wild-type cone currents show opposite pharmacology.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C6, C30-C31, C37, C39-C40, C48-C59 provide converging electrophysiological evidence from voltage-clamp recordings, pharmacological manipulations, and biophysical characterization across multiple species. The data consistently demonstrate Cav3 currents only in mutant mouse cones, with appropriate controls including double-pulse protocols, drug selectivity tests in HEK cells, and recordings from multiple species. Statistical analyses support the conclusions.

results.result: Cone synapses fail to form in Cav1.4 KO mice but are present in G369i KI mice, though with structural abnormalities including enlarged pedicles, elongated ribbons, and aberrant telodendria. These findings indicate that the Cav1.4 protein (independent of Ca2+ conductance) is required for cone synapse assembly, while Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are necessary for proper synaptic refinement.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12, C23-C28 are supported by immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy data (Figure 1) showing clear morphological differences between genotypes. The interpretation that Cav1.4 protein is required for assembly while Ca2+ signals refine structure is logically consistent with the comparative phenotypes of KO versus KI mice.

results.result: Molecular components of cone synapses (bassoon, GPR179, mGluR6, TRPM1) assemble in G369i KI mice but show altered sub-synaptic distribution with increased volume occupancy, lower intensity, and linear scaling with pedicle size. Electron microscopy reveals disorganized ribbons, multi-directional telodendria, and increased incorrect postsynaptic partnerships (35% vs 14% in WT), though approximately half of ribbons still form appropriate invaginating contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C75, C118 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 6) and serial block-face EM reconstructions (Figure 7, Table 2). The data include appropriate statistical comparisons and quantification of multiple parameters. The conclusion of subtle but significant morphological changes is well-supported by the convergent anatomical evidence.

results.result: Horizontal cells in G369i KI mice exhibit light-evoked ON and OFF responses that are significantly reduced compared to WT but present, while Cav1.4 KO mice show negligible responses. The responses are DNQX-sensitive, confirming glutamatergic transmission, though the transient nature of ON responses suggests inadequate cessation of glutamate release during light.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82, C14 are supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from horizontal cells (Figure 8) with appropriate pharmacological controls (DNQX). Statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA) confirm significant differences between genotypes. The interpretation of transient ON responses is reasonable given the biophysical properties of Cav3 channels.

results.result: K+-evoked Ca2+ signals in G369i KI cone terminals are significantly lower in amplitude (ΔF/F0=1.07±0.02) compared to WT (ΔF/F0=1.85±0.1, p<0.0001) and more transient. The reduced Ca2+ signals in G369i KI cones likely result from rapid inactivation of Cav3 channels and/or reduced intracellular Ca2+ release, suggesting that Cav3 channels nominally support Ca2+ signaling and synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 are supported by two-photon Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 9) with appropriate statistical analysis (unpaired t-test, repeated measures ANOVA). The interpretation linking reduced Ca2+ signals to Cav3 channel properties is consistent with known biophysics. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-14 terminals).

results.result: Electroretinography reveals that G369i KI mice have normal a-waves (indicating intact cone photoreceptors) and measurable b-waves that are significantly larger than Cav1.4 KO mice at high light intensities. Flicker responses show similar non-monotonic patterns to WT but with significantly reduced amplitude, and inverted responses at high illumination suggest cone-to-OFF bipolar cell transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93, C15 are supported by ERG recordings (Figure 10a-d) with appropriate statistical analyses (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests). The data demonstrate functional cone pathways in G369i KI mice. The interpretation of inverted flicker responses is speculative but reasonable given the known circuitry.

results.result: Behavioral testing using visible platform swim assays demonstrates that Cav1.4 KO mice are blind under both scotopic and photopic conditions, while G369i KI mice perform normally under photopic conditions but are impaired under scotopic conditions. This indicates that Cav3 channels can support cone synaptic responses sufficient for photopic visual behavior in G369i KI mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C94-C97 are supported by visible platform swim test data (Figure 10e-f) with appropriate statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA). Sample sizes are adequate (n=9-11 mice per genotype). The conclusion that Cav3 channels support photopic vision in G369i KI mice is well-supported by the behavioral data combined with electrophysiological evidence.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that Cacna1h (encoding Cav3.2) is the major Cav3 transcript in WT mouse cones, with no significant difference in expression between WT and G369i KI cones. This indicates that enhanced Cav3 channel activity in G369i KI cones results from post-transcriptional mechanisms rather than increased gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by drop-seq analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) with appropriate clustering and statistical comparison. The conclusion that post-transcriptional mechanisms account for enhanced Cav3 activity is logical given the lack of transcriptional changes, though the specific mechanisms remain unidentified.

results.result: The study proposes that in CSNB2, Cav3 channels maintain cone synaptic output through homeostatic plasticity, provided the non-conducting role of Cav1.4 in synaptogenesis remains intact. This represents a novel form of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity that relies on a non-canonical structural role of an ion channel, and G369i KI mice accurately model CSNB2 channelopathies with greater rod than cone pathway impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C98-C101, C138 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. The proposal is well-supported by the collective data showing: (1) Cav3 upregulation in both mutant models, (2) functional cone synapses only in G369i KI mice where Cav1.4 protein is present, and (3) preserved photopic vision in G369i KI mice. The interpretation is logical and consistent with all presented evidence.

results.result: The G369i mutation prevents Ca2+ permeation through Cav1.4, and the presence of synapses in G369i KI but not Cav1.4 KO mice demonstrates that the Cav1.4 protein (not its conductance) is required for synapse assembly. Cav1.4 interacts with multiple ribbon synapse-associated proteins and may pioneer ribbon assembly sites, though Cav3 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for this process.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22, C102-C108 are supported by prior work (cited Maddox et al., 2020) and the current anatomical data. The interpretation that Cav1.4 protein has a structural/scaffolding role is well-supported by the comparative phenotypes and is consistent with known protein-protein interactions (multiple citations provided).

results.result: Pharmacological characterization shows that isradipine significantly but incompletely suppresses ICa in WT cones without shifting voltage-dependence, suggesting residual current is from unblocked Cav1.4. ML 218 has modest non-significant effects on WT cone ICa but strongly inhibits Cav3.2 in HEK cells, indicating weak off-target activity on Cav1.4.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by pharmacological experiments in cones (Figure 3) and HEK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical analyses. The interpretation regarding drug selectivity is reasonable and important for validating the identification of Cav3 currents in mutant cones.

results.result: Drop-seq analysis confirms extremely low Cacna1h expression compared to Cacna1f in WT cones. The authors note that pharmacological identification of Cav3 channels can be confounded by off-target drug effects, but conclude that biophysical properties of isradipine-sensitive currents in WT cones resemble only Cav1, while ML 218-sensitive currents in G369i KI cones resemble only Cav3.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 are supported by RNA-seq data and comprehensive pharmacological/biophysical characterization across multiple experimental systems. The cautionary note about pharmacological interpretation (C110) demonstrates appropriate scientific rigor. The conclusion is well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: Despite similar peak ICa amplitudes near resting potential in WT and G369i KI cones, strong Cav3 inactivation and/or reduced intracellular Ca2+ release account for diminished Ca2+ signals in G369i KI pedicles. The enlarged synapses and increased connectivity errors may represent homeostatic compensation for weakened output. Balanced presynaptic Ca2+ signals appear necessary for proper cone synapse structure and wiring, and Cav3 channels are not optimally suited for supporting ribbon synapse transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C134 represent interpretations and mechanistic discussions supported by the experimental data and relevant literature (multiple citations). The reasoning is logical and consistent with known Ca2+ channel biophysics and synaptic organization principles. The speculative elements (C124-C126, C133) are appropriately qualified.

results.result: CSNB2 manifests as a spectrum of visual disorders from CACNA1F mutations, many producing non-conducting channels. G369i KI mice model CSNB2 channelopathies with greater rod than cone pathway impairment, exhibiting horizontal cell responses to bright illumination, ERG responses under light adaptation, and photopic but not scotopic visual behavior. Modest synaptic release combined with enlarged synapses and possible inner retinal compensation may support nominal cone pathway transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C143 synthesize the findings in the context of human disease with appropriate citations. The conclusion that G369i KI mice model CSNB2 is well-supported by the pattern of rod versus cone pathway deficits. The speculation about inner retinal compensation (C143) is appropriately qualified and cited.

results.result: Background information establishes that Cav1.4 mediates synaptic release from photoreceptors, exhibits slow inactivation suited for tonic glutamate release, and that over 200 CACNA1F mutations cause CSNB2. Rod and cone synapses fail to form in Cav1.4 KO mice, limiting their utility for studying CACNA1F mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C18-C20 represent established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The information is accurately presented.

results.result: Detailed biophysical characterization shows that ICa in WT cones activates around -50 mV and peaks near -20 mV (consistent with Cav1.4), while ICa in G369i KI cones shows hyperpolarized activation (~10 mV shift), rapid inactivation, and a sizeable window current—features resembling Cav3 T-type channels. The aberrant current is specific to cones, not rods.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C32-C36 are supported by voltage-clamp recordings (Figure 2, Table 1) with appropriate statistical analyses. The biophysical characterization is thorough and the comparison to known channel properties is well-founded. This provides critical evidence for identifying the aberrant current as Cav3-mediated.

results.result: A double-pulse protocol demonstrates that a prepulse to -60 mV reduces subsequent current amplitude in G369i KI cones (P2/P1 <1) but not in WT cones, consistent with voltage-dependent inactivation of Cav3 channels in mutant cones.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 2g-i) using an appropriate experimental design to test for Cav3 channel inactivation properties. The results clearly distinguish WT from G369i KI cones and support the presence of Cav3 channels in the latter.

results.result: The authors speculate that slow deactivation of Cav3 channels and/or their activation at negative voltages could generate Ca2+ signals supporting glutamate release following light-induced hyperpolarization in G369i KI cones.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is explicitly speculative and lacks direct experimental evidence. While the speculation is based on known Cav3 channel properties (cited), no experiments directly test this mechanism. The transient ON response in horizontal cells (C82) provides indirect support but is insufficient to confirm the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The Discussion notes that Cav3.2 is uniquely sensitive to post-translational modifications affecting channel opening and trafficking, including interactions with USP5 (suppressing degradation) and phosphorylation by CaMKII and CDK5 (enhancing activation and current density).
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C117 represent cited background information from the literature that provides potential mechanisms for enhanced Cav3 activity without increased transcription. The citations are appropriate and the information is accurately presented, though no experiments in this study directly test these mechanisms.

results.result: The study demonstrates that cone synapses fail to form in Cav1.4 KO mice (with shrunken pedicles retracted into the ONL and little evidence of ribbons), whereas in G369i KI mice, cone synapses are present but enlarged with some structural abnormalities including elongated ribbons and telodendria extending toward the inner nuclear layer. The authors conclude that Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for the integrity of ribbons and pedicles but necessary for their refinement.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating that 'the expression of a Cav1.4 variant lacking calcium conductivity supports the development of cone synapses beyond what is observed in the complete absence of Cav1.4' and that 'the evidence for the function of Cav1.4 protein in synapse development is convincing.' The differential analysis of mutant phenotypes is praised as a strength.

results.result: The authors report detection of Cav3 (T-type) Ca2+ currents in cones of G369i KI and Cav1.4 KO mice but not in wild-type mouse, ground squirrel, or macaque cones. These currents showed biophysical properties characteristic of Cav3 channels (low-voltage activation around -60 mV, rapid inactivation, hyperpolarizing shift in activation voltage). The authors conclude this represents an adaptation to Cav1.4 loss-of-function specifically in cones but not rods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding, noting that the study 'indicates that the cone pathway can partially operate even without calcium flux through Cav1.4 channels' and that 'further data indicate that Cav3 channels are present.' The broad methodological approaches including electrophysiology are cited as strengths, and the differential analysis is described as convincing.

results.result: Pharmacological characterization using isradipine (L-type blocker) and ML 218 (T-type blocker) demonstrated that ICa in WT cones was suppressed by isradipine but not ML 218, whereas in G369i KI cones, ML 218 nearly abolished ICa while isradipine had little effect. Ground squirrel and macaque cones showed no evidence of Cav3 currents, confirming Cav3 channels do not normally contribute to ICa in wild-type cones.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the study employed 'pharmacological manipulations' as part of the methodological portfolio and describe the evidence as 'convincing.' The differential responses to pharmacological agents support the identification of Cav3 channels in mutant but not wild-type cones, which reviewers accept as part of the overall findings.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that Cacna1h (encoding Cav3.2) was the major Cav3 transcript in WT mouse cones, with no significant difference in expression between WT and G369i KI cones. The authors conclude that enhanced Cav3 channel activity results from a mechanism other than increased transcription, representing upregulation of a Cav3 conductance as a common response to Cav1.4 loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the mechanism of compensation of Cav1.4 loss by Cav3 remains unclear but appears to involve post-transcriptional processes' and identify as a weakness that 'the mechanism by which Cav3 channels might partially compensate for the loss of Cav1.4 calcium currents remains unclear.' This indicates the evidence for the mechanism is insufficient.

results.result: Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy revealed that presynaptic and postsynaptic proteins assembled at cone synapses in G369i KI mice, but with altered sub-synaptic distribution: labeled structures occupied larger volumes with lower intensity, ribbons appeared disorganized and often parallel to the membrane, and a larger fraction of synaptic sites formed incorrect postsynaptic partnerships. The authors conclude cone synapses undergo relatively subtle morphological changes in response to loss of Cav1.4 Ca2+ signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm that 'expression of a nonconducting Cav1.4 channel mitigates these perturbations' and praise the 'convincing differential analysis of mutant phenotypes.' The use of 'serial block-face-SEM' and 'microscopic imaging' are cited as methodological strengths, indicating acceptance of the structural findings.

results.result: Electrophysiological recordings showed that Cav1.4 KO mice lack evidence of cone synaptic responses, whereas G369i KI mice exhibited nominal transmission from cones to horizontal cells and bipolar cells. Light responses in G369i KI horizontal cells were present but significantly reduced in amplitude compared to WT, with transient ON responses suggesting inadequate cessation of glutamate release.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that the study 'indicates that the cone pathway can partially operate even without calcium flux through Cav1.4 channels' and cite electrophysiology as part of the 'broad portfolio of methodological approaches.' The finding that some synaptic transmission is preserved is accepted as part of the overall evidence.

results.result: Ca2+ imaging experiments showed that K+-evoked Ca2+ signals in G369i KI cone terminals were significantly lower in amplitude than in WT cones. The authors conclude that Cav3 channels nominally support Ca2+ signals and synaptic transmission in G369i KI cones, though the lower amplitude and more transient signals may be cleared more rapidly than prolonged Cav1.4-initiated signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept that Cav3 channels 'may compensate for the loss of Cav1.4 calcium currents and thus maintain cone synaptic transmission,' indicating acceptance of the functional evidence. The methodological approaches including imaging are cited as strengths.

results.result: ERG recordings and behavioral tests demonstrated that Cav1.4 KO mice are blind with no visual behavior, whereas G369i KI mice exhibit normal photopic visual behavior, preserved ERG responses under light adaptation, and horizontal cell responses to bright illumination. Under scotopic conditions, both mutant strains showed impaired performance, but G369i KI mice performed as well as WT under photopic conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state the study 'indicates that the cone pathway can partially operate even without calcium flux through Cav1.4 channels, thus preserving behavioral responses under bright light.' The use of ERGs and behavioral testing are cited as methodological strengths, and the preservation of photopic function is accepted as a key finding.

results.result: The authors propose that in CSNB2, Cav3 channels maintain cone synaptic output provided that the nonconducting role of Cav1.4 in cone synaptogenesis remains intact. They conclude this reveals an unexpected form of homeostatic plasticity relying on a non-canonical role of an ion channel, and that G369i KI mice accurately model Cav1.4 channelopathies in CSNB2 patients.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the main conclusions, stating the study 'shows that the expression of a Cav1.4 variant lacking calcium conductivity supports the development of cone synapses' and 'indicates that the cone pathway can partially operate.' They note this 'helps to explain what functional defects exactly cause CSNB2 and why it is accompanied by only mild visual impairment,' indicating acceptance of the disease modeling interpretation.

results.result: The authors discuss that ribbons and synaptic components assemble at cone synapses in G369i KI mice, indicating Cav3 Ca2+ signals are dispensable for ribbon assembly. They propose Cav1.4 could pioneer sites of ribbon assembly by serving as a docking or nucleation site, supported by its interactions with ribbon-associated proteins and colocalization with ribbon precursor spheres.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that 'the evidence for the function of Cav1.4 protein in synapse development is convincing and in agreement with a closely related earlier study by the same authors on rod photoreceptors.' This indicates acceptance of the non-conducting role of Cav1.4 in synapse assembly.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms for Cav3.2 upregulation, noting that Cav3.2 is uniquely sensitive to post-translational modifications including interactions with USP5 (enhancing protein levels) and phosphorylation by CaMKII and CDK5 (enhancing channel activation and current density).
results.evaluation: While reviewers note the mechanism 'appears to involve post-transcriptional processes,' they explicitly state this 'remains unclear' as a weakness. The discussion of potential mechanisms is acknowledged but not validated, indicating the evidence is speculative rather than conclusive.

results.result: The authors discuss various aspects of how altered Ca2+ signals might affect synapse structure and function, including effects on ribbon size, synaptic scaling, postsynaptic wiring, and the efficiency of coupling to exocytosis. They propose that balanced presynaptic Ca2+ signals may be needed to encode correct postsynaptic wiring and that Cav3 channels' biophysical properties limit their ability to support sustained release.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the overall interpretation that structural and functional defects result from altered Ca2+ signaling, noting the study shows 'defects in cone synaptic transmission that correlate with aberrant cone synapse morphology.' The mechanistic discussions are treated as reasonable interpretations of the data.

results.result: Background claims about Cav1.4 function, CSNB2 disease characteristics, and the G369i mutation are presented as established knowledge from prior studies and citations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as established background, noting the work 'relates to a wide range of neuroscience topics, from synapse biology to neuro-ophthalmology' and that findings are 'in agreement with a closely related earlier study by the same authors.' No concerns are raised about the background information.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C9-C12, C23-C28 regarding cone synapse development and the structural role of Cav1.4 protein. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and supported, with reviewers explicitly affirming the differential phenotype analysis as a strength.

Perfect agreement on claims C63-C75, C118 regarding subtle morphological changes in cone synapses. Both evaluations support the findings based on immunofluorescence and EM data, with reviewers praising the differential analysis and microscopic imaging approaches.

Perfect agreement on claims C84-C89 regarding reduced Ca2+ signals in cone terminals. Both evaluations find the two-photon imaging data convincing and accept the functional interpretation linking reduced signals to Cav3 channel properties.

Disagreement on claims C114-C117 regarding post-transcriptional mechanisms. OpenEval finds the cited literature provides adequate support, while peer reviewers explicitly state the mechanism 'remains unclear' and identify this as a weakness, indicating insufficient evidence.

Agreement on claims C119-C133 regarding mechanistic interpretations of Ca2+ signaling effects. Both evaluations accept these as reasonable interpretations supported by the data and literature, with reviewers noting the correlation between structural and functional defects.

Agreement on claims C76-C82, C14 regarding horizontal cell responses and preserved synaptic transmission. Both evaluations find the electrophysiological evidence convincing, with reviewers accepting that cone pathways can partially operate in the mutant.

Agreement on claims C16-C17, C98-C101, C138 representing main conclusions. Both evaluations support the synthesis of findings, with reviewers affirming the study explains CSNB2 functional defects and the role of Cav1.4 protein in synapse development.

Agreement on claims C102-C107 regarding the non-conducting structural role of Cav1.4. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing, with reviewers noting agreement with prior work by the same authors on rod photoreceptors.

Disagreement on claims C60-C62 regarding post-transcriptional mechanisms. OpenEval finds the drop-seq analysis and logical inference sufficient, while peer reviewers explicitly state the mechanism 'remains unclear' and identify this as a weakness requiring further investigation.

Agreement on claims C2-C6, C30-C40 regarding Cav3 channel presence and electrophysiological characterization. Both evaluations find the voltage-clamp and pharmacological evidence convincing, with reviewers acknowledging the broad methodological approaches as strengths.

Agreement on claims C7-C8, C94-C97 regarding preserved photopic vision and behavioral responses. Both evaluations support the findings from ERG and behavioral testing, with reviewers explicitly stating the cone pathway can partially operate under bright light.

Agreement on claims C1, C18-C20 as established background knowledge. Both evaluations accept these as accurate context supported by appropriate citations, with no concerns raised about the background information.

Agreement on claims C41-C47 regarding pharmacological characterization of Cav3 channels. Both evaluations find the drug selectivity experiments convincing, with reviewers citing pharmacological manipulations as part of the methodological strengths.

Agreement on claims C29, C32-C36 regarding biophysical properties of the aberrant current. Both evaluations accept the voltage-clamp characterization as thorough and convincing for identifying Cav3-mediated currents.

Agreement on claims C90-C93, C15 regarding ERG recordings showing functional cone pathways. Both evaluations support the electrophysiological evidence, with reviewers accepting the preservation of some cone pathway function.

Agreement on claims C135-C137 regarding CSNB2 disease modeling. Both evaluations accept the synthesis in the disease context, with reviewers noting the study helps explain functional defects and mild visual impairment in CSNB2.

Agreement on claims C38-C40 regarding Cav3 channel inactivation properties. Both evaluations find the double-pulse protocol data convincing as part of the broader electrophysiological characterization supporting Cav3 channel identification.

Partial overlap on claim C113. OpenEval finds the RNA-seq and pharmacological evidence sufficient for identifying Cav3 channels, while peer reviewers accept the channel identification but note the compensatory mechanism remains unclear.

OpenEval identifies claim C83 as explicitly speculative regarding the mechanism of transient ON responses in horizontal cells, noting lack of direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this speculative claim.

Peer reviewers evaluate claim C13 regarding defects in cone synaptic transmission, which is not separately evaluated by OpenEval but is implicitly covered in broader evaluations of synaptic function (R4, R6).
